notes.definition: Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food, such as mycoprotein from the fungus Fusarium. Genetic modification is used to make useful products such as human insulin, and GM crops could provide more food or food with improved nutritional value, such as golden rice.
explanation: Biotechnology means using living organisms, especially microorganisms, to make useful products. Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured (grown) for food. Microorganisms grow and reproduce quickly, can be grown in large vessels called fermenters all year round, and need little land. This makes them a possible solution to the demands of a growing human population.

The fungus Fusarium is used to produce mycoprotein, a protein-rich food that is suitable for vegetarians because it does not come from animals. The fungus is grown in a fermenter on glucose syrup, which provides its energy source, in aerobic conditions: sterile air is bubbled in to supply oxygen for respiration. Conditions such as temperature and pH are kept at the optimum. The fungal biomass is then harvested and purified to produce mycoprotein, which can be made into foods such as meat substitutes.

Genetic modification (GM) can also help. A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. The human gene for insulin is inserted into the bacterium, which is then cultured in large numbers. When the insulin is harvested and purified it can be used to treat people with diabetes. This shows how culturing microorganisms on a large scale can provide useful products as well as food.

GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value. For example, crops can be modified to be resistant to insect pests or to herbicides, increasing yields. Golden rice is a variety of rice that has been genetically modified, using genes from another plant (maize) and a bacterium, so that its grains contain beta-carotene. The body uses beta-carotene to make vitamin A, so golden rice could reduce vitamin A deficiency, which causes blindness and illness in children in countries where rice is the main food.

When you describe and explain biotechnical and agricultural solutions to feeding the growing population, consider both benefits and concerns. Benefits include fast production, less land use, high-protein food without rearing animals, and better nutrition. Some people are concerned about GM crops, for example about possible effects on wild plants and insects if genes spread, possible effects on human health, and the cost of GM seed for poorer farmers. Mycoprotein production also needs energy and sterile conditions.
keyFacts: Modern biotechnology enables large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food.
The fungus Fusarium is used to produce mycoprotein.
Mycoprotein is a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians.
Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions.
The fungal biomass is harvested and purified to make mycoprotein.
A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin, used to treat diabetes after harvesting and purifying.
GM crops could provide more food or food with improved nutritional value.
Golden rice is GM rice containing beta-carotene, which the body uses to make vitamin A.

keyTerms.definition: Using living organisms, especially microorganisms, to make useful products such as food or medicines.
A protein-rich food made from the fungus Fusarium, suitable for vegetarians.
A fungus grown in fermenters on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions to produce mycoprotein.
A large vessel in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions (temperature, pH, oxygen) and kept sterile.
Changing the genome of an organism by inserting a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
Genetically modified rice whose grains contain beta-carotene, a substance the body uses to make vitamin A.
Conditions in which oxygen is available, so the microorganism can carry out aerobic respiration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mycoprotein is made from bacteria or from soya.
misconceptions.right: In fact mycoprotein is made from the fungus Fusarium, grown on glucose syrup.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Fusarium is grown without oxygen, like yeast making alcohol.
misconceptions.right: In fact Fusarium is grown in aerobic conditions, with sterile air supplied so it can respire aerobically and grow quickly.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think golden rice contains extra vitamin A added after harvest.
misconceptions.right: In fact the rice is genetically modified so its grains make beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the insulin made by GM bacteria is bacterial insulin.
misconceptions.right: In fact the bacteria contain the human insulin gene, so they make human insulin, which is harvested and purified to treat diabetes.

realWorld: Mycoprotein from Fusarium is sold in supermarkets as meat-free mince, pieces and burgers.
Almost all insulin used by people with diabetes is now human insulin made by genetically modified microorganisms.
Golden rice has been approved for growing in the Philippines, where vitamin A deficiency is a public health problem.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (mycoprotein production, GM bacteria making insulin and GM crops such as golden rice as solutions to food demand) is in separate Biology (8461) only. Combined Science students study genetic engineering in topic 6, but not this application to food production.
examTips: For mycoprotein, learn the four key points: Fusarium (a fungus), glucose syrup, aerobic conditions, harvested and purified.
Say mycoprotein is 'protein-rich' and 'suitable for vegetarians': both phrases come straight from the specification.
For golden rice, state it is genetically modified to contain beta-carotene (for vitamin A), giving improved nutritional value.
In evaluation questions on GM crops, give benefits (higher yield, better nutrition) and concerns (effects on wild plants and insects, human health, cost of seed), then conclude.
summary: Biotechnology lets large quantities of microorganisms be cultured for food.
Fusarium makes mycoprotein, a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians.
Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions, then harvested and purified.
GM bacteria make human insulin, which is harvested and purified to treat diabetes.
GM crops could give more food or more nutritious food.
Golden rice contains beta-carotene to help prevent vitamin A deficiency.

questions.question: What type of organism is Fusarium?
markScheme: 1 mark: a fungus
questions.explanation: Fusarium is a fungus. It is grown to make mycoprotein. Bacteria are used to make insulin, not mycoprotein.

questions.question: Which statement describes mycoprotein?
options: A meat product made from chicken
A protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians
markScheme: 1 mark: a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians
questions.explanation: Mycoprotein is made from the fungus Fusarium. It is rich in protein and contains no meat, so vegetarians can eat it.

questions.question: Golden rice is an example of a GM crop. How has it been improved?
options: Its grains contain beta-carotene, giving improved nutritional value
markScheme: 1 mark: its grains contain beta-carotene / improved nutritional value
questions.explanation: Golden rice was modified so its grains make beta-carotene, which the body uses to make vitamin A. It still needs water and still contains starch.

questions.question: What is Fusarium grown on to produce mycoprotein?
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose syrup
questions.explanation: Glucose syrup provides the fungus with its energy source. Using meat waste would make the product unsuitable for vegetarians.

questions.question: In what conditions is Fusarium grown in the fermenter?
options: In complete darkness with no glucose
markScheme: 1 mark: aerobic conditions
questions.explanation: Sterile air is bubbled through so the fungus can respire aerobically, releasing more energy for rapid growth. It is not an anaerobic fermentation like making alcohol.

questions.question: A genetically modified bacterium is used to produce which substance for treating diabetes?
markScheme: 1 mark: human insulin
questions.explanation: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria, which then make human insulin. Once harvested and purified it treats diabetes.

questions.question: What happens to the Fusarium biomass after it has grown in the fermenter?
options: It is fed to cattle to make beef
It is left to decay in the fermenter
markScheme: 1 mark: it is harvested and purified
questions.explanation: The fungal biomass is harvested and purified to make mycoprotein for human food. Feeding it to cattle would add a trophic level and waste biomass.

markScheme: 1 mark: to prevent other microorganisms contaminating the culture (competing or making harmful substances)
questions.explanation: Contaminating microorganisms would compete for glucose and might produce toxins, making the food unsafe. Sterility does not control temperature or stop respiration.

questions.question: Which of these is a concern that some people have about growing GM crops?
options: GM crops always have lower yields
Genes from GM crops could spread to wild plants and affect wildlife
GM crops do not need sunlight
markScheme: 1 mark: genes could spread to wild plants and affect wildlife
questions.explanation: A common concern is that inserted genes may spread to wild relatives or affect insect populations. GM crops are usually grown for higher yields, are eaten, and still need light for photosynthesis.

questions.question:
Complete the sentence.
Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be
markScheme: 1 mark: cultured for food
questions.explanation: The specification states that biotechnology enables large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food, such as mycoprotein.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mass of protein in 100 g of two foods.
Calculate the mass of protein in a 250 g portion of mycoprotein.

headers: Mass of protein in 100 g of food in g

markScheme: 1 mark: 27.5 g
questions.explanation: 250 g is 2.5 lots of 100 g, so 2.5 × 11 = 27.5 g of protein.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the yields of two varieties of maize.
Calculate the percentage increase in yield when the GM pest-resistant variety is grown instead of the non-GM variety.
markScheme: 1 mark: 25%
questions.explanation: Increase = 0.8 tonnes per hectare. 0.8 ÷ 3.2 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by 4.0 would give 20%, which is wrong because you must divide by the original value.

questions.question:
A fermenter produces 300 kg of Fusarium biomass every hour.
Calculate the mass of biomass produced in 24 hours.
questions.explanation: 300 kg per hour × 24 hours = 7200 kg. Fermenters can run continuously, producing large quantities of food.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about a batch of dry mycoprotein.
Calculate the mass of protein in the batch.

headers: Dry mass of mycoprotein in kg
Percentage of dry mass that is protein

markScheme: 1 mark: 540 kg
questions.explanation: 45% of 1200 kg = 0.45 × 1200 = 540 kg of protein.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mass of protein in 100 g of beef and in 100 g of mycoprotein.
Calculate the mass of mycoprotein that contains the same mass of protein as 150 g of beef.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

headers: Mass of protein in 100 g of food in g

markScheme: 1 mark: protein in beef = 150 × 26 ÷ 100 = 39 g
1 mark: 355 g (3 s.f.)
questions.explanation: 39 g of protein is needed. Each gram of mycoprotein has 0.11 g of protein, so 39 ÷ 0.11 = 354.5... = 355 g to 3 significant figures.

questions.question: Name the fungus used to produce mycoprotein.
markScheme: 1 mark: Fusarium
questions.explanation: Fusarium is the fungus named in the specification.

questions.question: Explain why mycoprotein is suitable for vegetarians.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is made from a fungus, not from animals
questions.explanation: Vegetarians do not eat meat. Mycoprotein comes from fungal biomass grown on glucose syrup.

questions.question: State the substance that golden rice grains contain because of genetic modification.
markScheme: 1 mark: beta-carotene (allow: substance used to make vitamin A)
questions.explanation: Golden rice contains beta-carotene, which gives it its golden colour and is converted to vitamin A in the body.

1 mark: for aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the fungus to grow (allow: mixes the contents)
questions.explanation: Fusarium is grown in aerobic conditions. Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic, allowing rapid growth. Sterile air avoids contamination.

questions.question: Explain how GM crops could help to feed a growing human population.
markScheme: 1 mark: GM crops could provide more food, e.g. higher yields from pest or herbicide resistance
1 mark: or food with improved nutritional value, e.g. golden rice with beta-carotene
questions.explanation: The specification gives two benefits: more food, and more nutritious food.

questions.question: Describe how human insulin is produced using a genetically modified bacterium.
markScheme: 1 mark: the human insulin gene is inserted into a bacterium
1 mark: the bacteria are cultured / grown in large numbers (in a fermenter)
1 mark: the insulin is harvested and purified (then used to treat diabetes)
questions.explanation: This is an example of culturing large quantities of microorganisms to make a useful product.

questions.question: Suggest three advantages of producing protein as mycoprotein rather than by rearing cattle.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: fungus grows / reproduces quickly; needs little land / space; can be produced all year in controlled conditions; fungus is fed glucose directly, avoiding biomass losses of an extra trophic level (no energy lost to movement or keeping warm); suitable for vegetarians; no animal welfare concerns
questions.explanation: Rearing cattle loses most of the biomass in their food through respiration and egestion. Fusarium converts glucose into protein-rich biomass quickly in a small space.

questions.question:
In some countries many children have diets based mainly on rice and suffer from vitamin A deficiency.
Explain how golden rice could help.
markScheme: 1 mark: golden rice contains beta-carotene
1 mark: which the body converts to vitamin A, reducing vitamin A deficiency (and related blindness)
questions.explanation: Golden rice improves the nutritional value of a staple food, so people get vitamin A from the food they already eat.

questions.question: Give two concerns some people have about growing GM crops.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: genes may spread to wild plants; effects on wild insect populations / wildlife; possible effects on human health / long-term effects not fully known; cost of GM seed for poorer farmers
questions.explanation: Evaluation questions on GM crops expect concerns as well as benefits.

questions.question: Name the hormone produced by genetically modified bacteria that is used to treat diabetes.
markScheme: 1 mark: (human) insulin
questions.explanation: GM bacteria carry the human insulin gene and make human insulin.

questions.question:
The human population is increasing.
Describe and evaluate how biotechnology, including genetic modification, could help to meet the demand for food.
markScheme: Indicative content (descriptions):
large quantities of microorganisms can be cultured for food
Fusarium grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions in fermenters
biomass harvested and purified to make mycoprotein: protein-rich, suitable for vegetarians
GM crops could provide more food, e.g. pest or herbicide resistance increases yield
GM crops could give improved nutritional value, e.g. golden rice contains beta-carotene for vitamin A
Indicative content (evaluation):
microorganisms grow quickly, all year round, using little land
mycoprotein avoids biomass losses of rearing animals
fermenters need energy, sterile conditions and glucose, which must be grown
concerns about GM crops: genes spreading to wild plants, effects on insects, long-term health effects, cost of seed
conclusion: a justified judgement
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): both mycoprotein and GM crops described accurately, with advantages and concerns weighed and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both solutions described with some advantages or concerns.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one solution described simply.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: 'Evaluate' needs both sides and a conclusion. Accurate detail (Fusarium, glucose syrup, aerobic, harvested and purified, golden rice) is what earns the higher levels.

questions.question: Describe how mycoprotein is produced.
markScheme: Indicative content:
the fungus Fusarium is used
grown in large quantities in a fermenter
on glucose syrup (energy source)
in aerobic conditions: sterile air / oxygen supplied
temperature and pH kept at optimum; fermenter kept sterile
the fungal biomass is harvested
and purified to produce mycoprotein, a protein-rich food
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear sequence including Fusarium, glucose syrup, aerobic conditions, harvesting and purification.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points, e.g. made from a fungus.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The four specification points (Fusarium, glucose syrup, aerobic, harvested and purified) are the core of a full-mark answer.
